authors: Atul Singh Arora (University of Maryland, USA; Caltech, USA), Kishor Bharti (Agency for Science, Technology and Research (A*STAR), Singapore), Alexandru Cojocaru (University of Edinburgh, UK; University of Maryland, USA), Andrea Coladangelo (University of Washington, USA)

The fact that such a k is computationally indistinguishable from the correct one (from the point of view of the prover A) follows precisely from the security of the OPad. General Compilers: The compiler we described earlier handles contextuality games with contexts of size 2. How does one generalise it to contexts of arbitrary size? Unlike for KLVY, it is not entirely clear what the “correct” way is here. We design two compilers (which seem incomparable). The first compiler applies universally to all contextuality games. The second applies primarily to contextuality games where the quantum value is 1 (for instance, it works for the magic square but not for KCBS). Notably, both compilers are 4-message protocols.

We make some brief remarks about the two compilers and defer the details to the main text. (|C| − 1, 1) compiler: – Round 1: Ask |C| − 1 questions under QFHE. – Round 2: Ask 1 uniformly random question in the clear. If the question was already asked in Round 1, check consistency. Otherwise, check the predicate. • (|C|, 1) compiler – Round 1: Ask all |C| questions under QFHE. – Round 2: Ask 1 uniformly random question in the clear, and check consistency with the questions asked in Round 1. By now, one would be wary of guessing that asking more questions under QFHE is going to improve the security of the protocol.
